opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there's an interesting tension here. A lot of the theoretical framing in alignment, inherited from economics and decision theory, says an aligned AI is one that satisfies human preferences, or maximizes some utility function that represents them. That framing quietly assumes preferences are coherent, stable, and the right thing to aim at.

When you look at how language models are actually trained, especially with RLHF and its descendants, you see that framing in a very compressed form. We collect pairwise comparisons, "this response is better than that one," fit a reward model, usually something like Bradley-Terry, and optimize the policy against it. So the preferentialist picture is baked into the pipeline. But the data doesn't really behave that way. Annotators disagree. Their judgments depend on framing, on how tired they are, on what they think the task is. A comparison often stands in for a bundle of things: helpfulness, honesty, tone, whether it follows some policy. Collapsing all that into one scalar reward loses most of the structure.

Meanwhile, practitioners have moved toward something else without always saying so. Think of constitutions, model specs, and content policies. Those aren't preferences in the economic sense. They're closer to norms: standards for what an assistant in a particular role should and shouldn't do, which people can reason about, contest, and revise. I think that's healthier, and theory should catch up. Rather than "align the AI to the preferences of the user" or "of humanity," we might say an AI should be aligned to the normative standards appropriate to its social role, standards that come from the people it affects through legitimate processes.

So the gap is partly that theory oversimplifies human values, and partly that practice has already outgrown its theory without a good account of what it's doing. Closing it means taking seriously that human values are richer than a reward function. They involve reasons, commitments, and norms we hold each other to, and we should design training objectives and evaluation around that richer picture.

r001.rationale: The response describes preference theory as assuming judgments are coherent and stable, then connects pairwise comparisons to a Bradley–Terry reward model and scalar optimization. This communicates an underlying ordered preference model.

r002.rationale: It says scalar rewards lose the structure in human judgments, but does not explain that overoptimizing this imperfect proxy can fail to deliver what people want.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention keeping a reward-trained model close to its base policy or contrast that constraint with unconstrained expected-utility maximization.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the gap is actually pretty striking once you look at it closely, and it's one of the main things that motivated the work I did with my co-authors on what we called "Beyond Preferences in AI Alignment."

If you read the alignment literature, especially the more formal or philosophical side of it, there's this very dominant framing where the goal is to get an AI system to learn and satisfy human preferences. You see it in inverse reinforcement learning, in cooperative inverse RL, in the way people talk about value learning. And the underlying assumption, often implicit, is that human values can be adequately represented as preferences, usually in the expected utility sense, and that alignment means getting the system's objective to match those preferences, or some aggregate of them.

But then if you look at how people actually train language models, it looks quite different. Yes, RLHF uses something called a preference model, and that terminology does a lot of work in making it seem like the theory and the practice line up. But what's really happening is that annotators are asked to compare two outputs and pick the one that better follows a set of guidelines. Those guidelines are written by the developer. They say things like, be helpful, be honest, don't produce harmful content, follow the user's instructions unless they conflict with these other norms. So the "preferences" being learned are not really anyone's preferences in the economic sense. They're judgments about compliance with a set of norms and standards of behavior.

And I think that's actually the right thing to be doing, in a sense. The developers are, maybe without fully theorizing it, treating the model as something more like a role-bearing agent that should follow norms appropriate to its role as an assistant, rather than as a utility maximizer trying to satisfy the user's desires. If you look at something like constitutional AI, that's even more explicit. You're writing down principles in natural language and asking the model to critique and revise its outputs against them.

So the gap, as I see it, is that the theory says alignment is about preference satisfaction, and the practice has quietly moved toward alignment as norm-following and role-appropriate behavior. And I think the practice is closer to the truth about what we actually want from these systems. Preferences are a thin representation of human values. They flatten away the structure of what people care about, the reasons behind choices, the social and moral norms that constrain what counts as acceptable behavior. When you try to compress all of that into a reward signal, you lose things, and you also end up with these well-known pathologies like sycophancy, where the model learns that what gets rewarded is what people say they like in the moment rather than what actually serves them.

Where I think the gap becomes a problem is that because the theory hasn't caught up, we don't have good conceptual tools for asking the questions that matter. What norms should an AI assistant follow? Who gets to decide? How do you handle disagreement across people and cultures about those norms? Those are questions about legitimacy and about normative standards, not about aggregating preferences. And if we keep describing the project in preference language, we end up either ignoring those questions or trying to force them into a framework that wasn't built for them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses preference satisfaction and comparisons between outputs, but it does not identify the theory’s assumption of a linear ordering of outputs.

r002.rationale: It describes sycophancy and how a reward signal can miss what serves people, but does not explain that overoptimizing a preference-learned reward function fails because it is an imperfect proxy.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention a constraint that reward-trained models stay close to the original base policy or contrast that constraint with unconstrained expected-utility maximization.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a gap between preferences as a theoretical concept and preferences as a training signal. In a lot of alignment theory, we imagine that a person has some underlying preferences, and the problem is to infer those preferences and then act in ways that satisfy them. But when developers train language models using human feedback, they’re typically collecting judgments about particular responses: which of these two answers is better?

That judgment doesn’t necessarily express a preference over how the world should turn out. It might express whether an answer is truthful, whether it follows an instruction, whether it’s appropriate in context, or whether the assistant is doing its job well. Calling all of those things “preferences” can obscure the different kinds of reasoning involved.

For example, I might judge that an assistant should help you accomplish something even though it’s not something I personally want. I’m evaluating its behavior in relation to your goals and its role, rather than asking it to optimize the world according to my desires.

So I think the practical training process is doing something closer to teaching models norms of good assistance. Preference comparisons are one way to communicate those norms, but that doesn’t mean preference satisfaction is the right account of what we’re ultimately trying to achieve. We need a theory that takes seriously how people understand instructions, responsibilities, and the limits of what they’re authorized to do.

r001.rationale: The response describes underlying preferences and judgments comparing answers, but does not say that preference-based theory assumes a linear ordering of outputs.

r002.rationale: It questions whether preference satisfaction is the right account, but does not explain that overoptimizing a learned reward function can fail because it is an imperfect proxy for what people want.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention keeping reward-trained models close to the original base policy or contrast that constraint with unconstrained expected-utility maximization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a gap between preferences as a theoretical account of what we want an AI system to do and preferences as a source of training data. In a lot of alignment theory, we imagine that a person has some underlying preference ordering, and the problem is to infer it and then optimize for it. But when developers collect preferences for language models, they’re typically asking people to compare two responses. Which one is more helpful? Which one is more accurate? Which one follows the instructions better?

Those judgments don’t necessarily reveal a single, stable objective that the person wants maximized. Someone might prefer one response because it respects a boundary, or because it’s appropriate to the role the assistant is playing. So the judgment can be about norms, obligations, or context, rather than simply about which outcome they like more.

And the training process combines those judgments with demonstrations, written policies, and other forms of feedback. I think it’s useful to understand that as teaching a system how to act within a set of human practices. Preference feedback is one tool for doing that, but it doesn’t mean that preference maximization is the best account of what we’re trying to achieve.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes an assumed underlying preference ordering, but does not specify that it is a linear ordering of outputs.

r002.rationale: It says preference judgments may not capture a stable objective, but does not explain how overoptimizing a learned reward as an imperfect proxy can fail to deliver what people want.

r003.rationale: It does not mention keeping reward-trained models close to the base policy or contrast that constraint with unconstrained expected-utility maximization.
